nameStory: This rare plant honors Kate Furbish, a pioneering Maine botanist and botanical artist who first discovered and identified it as a new species in 1880. She originally called it Furbish's wood betony, but today we know it as Furbish's lousewort - part of a plant family with the unfortunate name 'lousewort' from old folk beliefs that these plants caused lice in livestock.
description: Furbish's lousewort is a perennial herb that grows along the rocky shores of the upper Saint John River in northern Maine. This endangered wildflower is one of New England's rarest plants, found nowhere else on Earth except this specific river corridor and adjacent New Brunswick. It's a medium-sized plant that emerges from the same spot year after year, perfectly adapted to its unique riverbank home.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively on the shores of the upper Saint John River in northern Maine - if you're not along this specific river system, you're not looking at Furbish's lousewort

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular, two-lipped flowers typical of the lousewort family, with an upper hooded lip and lower three-lobed lip, arranged in dense spikes

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, fern-like leaves that feel soft to the touch and are arranged alternately along the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Perennial herb that returns from the same root system each year, growing in scattered colonies along the riverbank

habitat: Exclusively found on the shores and banks of the upper Saint John River in northern Maine, particularly in areas with periodic flooding and scouring. This highly specialized habitat includes rocky shores, gravel bars, and riverside terraces that experience the river's seasonal flood cycles.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the snow melts and river levels change, with distinctive fern-like foliage unfurling.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and blooming season, when the characteristic tubular flowers appear in dense spikes above the ferny leaves.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back as temperatures drop and the growing season ends along the northern river corridor.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant above ground, surviving as underground roots and waiting for spring's return.

funFact: This plant is a real-life 'Lazarus species' - once thought to be completely extinct, it was dramatically rediscovered decades later, rising from the botanical dead to remind us that nature still holds secrets even in well-studied New England!
confusionNotes: Given its incredibly restricted range along just one river system, if you think you've found Furbish's lousewort anywhere else in New England, you're likely looking at a different plant entirely - probably a fern or another member of the lousewort family.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the unfortunate name 'lousewort,' these plants don't actually cause lice - that's just an old superstition. The scientific name honors both Kate Furbish, a remarkable woman botanist working in the 1800s when few women were recognized in science, and represents one of New England's most important botanical discoveries.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives Canadian lousewort and swamp lousewort which grow in various habitats throughout New England, Furbish's lousewort is completely restricted to one river system. Canadian lousewort prefers dry woods and fields, while swamp lousewort grows in wetlands - but Furbish's needs the very specific conditions of the Saint John River's dynamic shoreline.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canadian lousewort is the most common and widespread lousewort in New England, while its relatives are much rarer.

Swamp lousewort differs from Canadian lousewort by its wetland habitat (Canadian lousewort prefers dry woods and fields) and its cream-colored flowers in a tight spiral versus Canadian lousewort's yellow and red flowers in a looser cluster.
